background.definition: Raynaud's phenomenon is a reversible vasospasm of arteries and arterioles within acral body segments precipitated primarily by cold or emotional stress. The ischemic phase appears as white/blanching or blue skin and ends as erythematous skin (reactive hyperemia). Primary Raynaud's is characterized by a long history of attacks (typically since adolescence), mild to moderate symptoms, and a lack of complications or tissue damage from ischemia. The secondary form is associated with connective tissue disorders, especially systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).

list.listitem: 2.2% in women in US community-based population.
1.5% in men in US community-based population.
Primary Raynaud's has no known etiology.
Secondary Raynaud's is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (e.g., systemic sclerosis), peripheral vascular disease, Buerger's disease, or paraneoplastic disorders.
Secondary Raynaud's may also be caused by repetitive vibration from occupational exposure.
The effect of alcohol appears to vary with the amount and type of alcohol, as well as gender of the drinker.
The prevalence of Raynaud's among patients on beta-blocker therapy is 14.7%.
Imbalance between vasoactive and vasoconstrictive regulation of the blood vessel wall, favoring vasoconstriction.

Primary Raynaud's displays functional vascular defects compared with Raynaud's due to systemic sclerosis, which displays structural and functional defects in the endothelium early in the disease process that progress to pronounced intimal thickening, possibly leading to complete occlusion.

list.listitem: Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by pale or cyanotic digits triggered by cold or stress, sometimes associated with pain or numbness, and followed by reactive hyperemia upon rewarming. C
Determine whether Raynaud's phenomenon is secondary to other disease (e.g., systemic sclerosis) or primary in origin. C
Useful diagnostic tests if secondary Raynaud's is suspected include thoracic outlet test, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), antinuclear antibodies (ANAs), and nail capillary dermoscopy. C

Patients typically present with episodic, recurrent vasospastic episodes consisting of triphasic color change in the fingers and/or toes associated with cold temperature or stress. Pallor leads to cyanosis and accompanying pain and numbness with flushing and redness noted on rewarming. The nose, ears, tongue, and nipples may also be involved. Some patients may have only 2 phases, pallor and then cyanosis.
Onset is most commonly between 15 and 30 years.

Take a history for occupational exposure to mechanical vibration such as pneumatic equipment, a history for other symptoms of autoimmune or collagen vascular disease, and for any family history of Raynaud's or autoimmune diseases.

Examine the patient for signs of secondary causes including pulse palpation in the upper limbs. Inspect skin of hands and feet for signs of connective tissue disease (thickening, tightening, induration, sclerosis, sclerodactyly, digital pitting scars, loss of digital pad tissue, or digital tissue necrosis). Palpate pulses in the upper limbs for thoracic outlet syndrome.

Perform nail capillaroscopy by applying mineral oil to the nailfold and examining under a high diopter (>20) with a direct ophthalmoscope. Look for pathologic capillaries; torturous, enlarged capillaries are easily seen, whereas normal capillaries are not with this method. Abnormal capillary appearance is specific for systemic sclerosis.
No specific diagnostic test exists for confirming the diagnosis of Raynaud's phenomenon. It is based on history and physical examination findings alone.

Diagnostic tests are helpful when secondary Raynaud's is suspected based on the history and physical: ANA, ESR, CRP, cryoglobulin level, antistreptolysin antibodies, anticentromere antibodies, and rheumatoid factor.
Perform CXR for underlying lung or cardiac pathology if clinically indicated (e.g., abnormal lung examination, pulmonary symptoms, rheumatoid nodules).
Order radiographs of the hands if the patient has joint pain to look for soft tissue changes, calcification, or bony erosions.
Patients present with triphasic color change in fingers and/or toes associated with cold temperature or stress.

Ascertain the presence of underlying autoimmune disease, occupational exposures to repetitive vibrations, and tobacco and alcohol use. Inspect the skin of hands and feet for signs of connective tissue changes.
Perform laboratory and radiologic studies to distinguish further between secondary and primary Raynaud's as clinically indicated.
Consider acrocyanosis, characterized by continuous, nonperiodic cyanosis that worsens with cold exposure, and peripheral vascular disease in the differential diagnosis.
Calcium channel antagonists improve symptoms in primary Raynaud's. B
Topical nitrates and phosphodiesterase inhibitors are recommended as second line therapy.B
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) may have modest benefit in relieving symptoms but are not superior to calcium channel antagonists. B
Alternative therapies such as thermal biofeedback, and Ginkgo biloba extract may improve symptoms of primary Raynaud's. B
Consider referring patients with suspected autoimmune disorders to a rheumatologist. C

First-line drug therapy: nifedipine, a calcium channel antagonist. Use 10 to 30 mg 3 times daily or the long-acting form, starting at 30 mg daily, with slow titration of the dose upward to relieve symptoms. Nifedipine shows modest efficacy in reducing the severity and frequency of Raynaud's ischemic attacks (average of 2.8-5.0 fewer attacks per week and 33% reduction in severity of attacks).
Amlodipine 5 to 20 mg/day is also effective as first-line therapy.

Topical nitroglycerin reduces the severity of attacks. A systematic review of 7 RCTs found evidence of a moderate to large treatment effect with topical nitrates in both sporadic (primary) and secondary Raynaud's.

A meta-analysis of RCTs concluded that phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) decrease Raynaud's Condition Scores (RCS) and the daily frequency and duration of attacks.
ACEIs and ARBs may provide some benefit in relief of Raynaud's phenomenon, although no good evidence shows that they are superior to calcium channel antagonists.

A small randomized crossover trial of 29 patients with Raynaud's associated with connective tissue diseases found no difference in the frequency of Raynaud's attacks between amlodipine (10 mg/d) and udenafil 100 mg/day.

Treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon due to systemic sclerosis includes α-blockers (e.g., prazosin), prostacyclin analogues (iloprost), endothelin receptor agonists (bosentan), and phosphodiesterase inhibitors (sildenafil).
IV iloprost 0.5 to 2.0 ng/kg/minute over 6 hours daily for 5 days is recommended for patients with acute ischemic injury to their digits.

A Cochrane review identified 15 RCTs with 635 patients comparing oral vasodilators to placebo. There is no evidence of benefit from oral vasodilators (e.g., captopril, beraprost, dazoxiben, ketanserin) in the treatment of either primary or secondary Raynaud's, and a Cochrane review concluded that their use may actually worsen symptoms.

Existing studies of thermal biofeedback are of low to moderate quality and show that it may help primary Raynaud's patients in reducing severity and frequency of attacks. However, a meta-analysis of 5 trials of biofeedback did not show effectiveness.

Standardized Ginkgo biloba extract (Seredrin) reduced the number of Raynaud's attacks by 56% (from 13 to 6 per week) in patients with primary Raynaud's compared with only 27% reduction in patients using placebo.
In a RCT, nifedipine was more effective than Ginkgo biloba (50.1% improvement at 8 weeks vs. 31.0%, respectively).

In a double-blind, randomized study of 76 patients with Raynaud's, wearing gloves for 6 weeks decreased the Raynaud's Condition Score by 2.5 points (minimal clinically significant difference 1.4 points). However no difference was noted between those wearing silver fiber gloves vs control (normal) gloves.

A systematic review identified 6 RCTs with 272 participants evaluating acupuncture for Raynaud's. Remission was more likely with acupuncture (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.31) and the daily number of attacks was decreased (weighted mean difference -0.57 attacks, 95% CI = -1.14 to -0.01). However, the quality of studies was poor and they were judged to be at high risk of bias.
A large placebo response has been observed in a study of n of 1 trials and a network meta-analysis, although regression to the mean is also likely occurring.
If collagen vascular disease is suspected, consider referral to a rheumatologist for further diagnosis and management.
About 1% of patients with primary Raynaud's transition to secondary Raynaud's each year. B
Patients with higher age at onset of symptoms, shorter duration of symptoms, and abnormal thoracic outlet testing have a higher risk of transitioning to secondary Raynaud's. B
